problems.description: 8 naming-convention violations across 4 files (app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, test_app.py): classes not PascalCase, module-level constants not UPPER_CASE, functions not snake_case — convention score 0.71.

app.py keeps flat routes with inline SQL while a separate tasks.py/repositories.py layer also exists, leaving the data-access path split across two places and the layering ambiguous for later story sessions.

Discrepancy in the mechanical measurements: AST diff reports +0 classes yet the convention check flags non-PascalCase classes in 4 files — the class count and naming checks disagree and should be reconciled.

strengths: SonarQube: smells -2, cognitive complexity -6, bugs +0 — the code is materially simpler than the seed it replaces.
Drops the low-quality legacy seed (hardcoded static password salt, dead migration helper, duplicate token helpers) without introducing new bugs.
Adds a test suite (test_app.py) and a repository layer (repositories.py) as scaffolding for the remaining story sessions.
Validates the title field and returns correct 400/201 status codes with clean JSON responses.
commit_reviews.summary: A simpler, statically cleaner greenfield rewrite of the seed into a task API, but its 8 naming-convention violations and split app.py/module layering represent debt that will compound across the remaining story sessions.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-key' when the env var is unset, making JWT tokens forgeable if deployed without configuration.
The additive migration leaves legacy rows with NULL owner_id, so pre-existing tasks become invisible to all users after scoping is enforced.
Visible tests cover register/login/auth-required flows but no cross-user isolation test asserting user B cannot read/modify user A's tasks.
Auth context is attached by mutating request.user_id/request.username on the global request object, a common but implicit Flask pattern.
Measured convention score of 0.71 is driven mostly by pre-existing violations in files outside this diff (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py), not by the code added here.

strengths: Additive migration (ALTER TABLE) preserves existing data rather than dropping/recreating
Owner-scoping applied to every task endpoint, closing cross-user access by default
Standard JWT flow with correct 401 handling for missing/invalid tokens and 409 on duplicate usernames
Reuses existing patterns (get_db, _row_to_task, route style) and adds type hints on new public signatures
Tests refactored into reusable fixtures (token, auth) and updated to exercise the authenticated path
wraps() preserves decorator metadata
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, idiomatic feature addition that scopes tasks to authenticated users with a data-preserving migration and standard JWT plumbing, though the low measured convention score stems from pre-existing violations in files untouched by this commit.

problems.description: send_notification_email.delay() is called inline with no broker-failure handling. If Redis is unavailable, the already-committed task UPDATE makes the PUT /tasks request return 500 and the notification is silently lost — a core write path is coupled to background infra. Wrap in try/except (log + continue) as is done in other story sessions (e.g. artifact 4d3aa8025ff3).

user_email falls back to request.username when no email is registered (email = ... or request.username). Username-as-email is semantically wrong; prefer None or an explicit placeholder so the task decides, rather than sending to 'alice'.
Tests mock delay and therefore never exercise the broker-failure path (delay raising), leaving the unhandled-exception fragility above untested.

strengths: Delivers exactly the Session 3 integration spec: Celery + Redis broker, send_notification_email(user_email, task_title), trigger from PUT /tasks/{id}, celery_config.py with broker URL/result backend/task routes.
Transition detection (row['status'] != 'completed' and updated['status'] == 'completed') correctly suppresses duplicate notifications on re-completing an already-completed task.
Additive migration for the users.email column follows the existing migrate() pattern and preserves existing data.
Tests are thorough and Redis-free: they monkeypatch delay to verify trigger logic, registered-email usage, no-notification-on-unchanged-status, duplicate suppression, and the task itself via apply()
Idiomatic Celery config: JSON serializers, UTC, explicit named 'email' queue via task_routes; type hints + docstrings on new public functions.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, spec-faithful async-notification integration with correct transition semantics and solid tests, slightly dragged by unhandled broker-coupling on the core write path; the measured convention score of 0.71 is deflated by checker false positives (the 8 flagged violations cite classes/constants in files that define none, plus repositories.py which this diff never touches), so qualitative convention adherence is notably higher.

problems.description: BaseRepository builds SQL via f-string interpolation of table/column names (create/update/get_by_id). Safe today because callers pass hardcoded keys, but it is a latent SQL-injection/fragility footgun if keys ever become dynamic. SonarQube reported +0 smells, so this is a qualitative flag, not a measured regression.

`table_name = abstractmethod(lambda self: None)` is an obscure way to declare an abstract class attribute; a @property + @abstractmethod or __init_subclass__ would be clearer and less surprising to future readers.
`isinstance(get_db, type(lambda: None))` is a roundabout callable check; the idiomatic `callable(get_db)` is clearer and avoids relying on lambda type identity.

Repositories are instantiated at module level (`task_repo = TaskRepository(get_db)`), coupling them to the Flask app's `get_db` at import time. Functional here (lazy callable) but limits dependency injection and unit-testing of the data layer in isolation.

Measured convention score is 0.71 with 8 violations, but the newly added code is largely compliant: all 3 new classes use PascalCase (BaseRepository, TaskRepository, UserRepository) and functions use snake_case. The flagged violations are concentrated in pre-existing files (celery_config.py, tasks.py, test_app.py, app.py); only repositories.py appears in the new diff, and its sole flag (module-level UPPER_CASE) is questionable given no obvious module-level constant was added.

strengths: Behavior-preserving refactor: SonarQube delta shows +0 bugs, +0 smells, +0.0% duplications, and the diff rewrites route handlers 1:1 with equivalent logic.
Centralizes all SQLite access behind a repository layer (BaseRepository/TaskRepository/UserRepository), making handlers declarative and the data layer independently unit-testable.
Net -58 lines while removing repeated `with get_db()` blocks from 5 route handlers, reducing boilerplate and duplicated queries.
Preserves existing patterns — still uses the `get_db` factory, `token_required` decorator, and `_row_to_task` helper — while keeping the `update_task` validation logic intact.
Clean ABC contract for the base repository with two focused concrete subclasses, an idiomatic and conventional layering for a small Flask app.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, behavior-preserving repository-pattern refactor that centralizes SQLite access and removes route-handler boilerplate, with only minor maintainability smells in the generic base class and a low convention score driven mostly by pre-existing violations rather than this commit's new code.

problems.description: GET /tasks response contract changed from a bare list to an envelope ({data, next_cursor, total}) — a breaking API change. Contained here (tests updated), but any other consumer of the old shape will break; verify no frontend/CLI/email-script callers exist.
list_tasks handler grows nested limit/cursor validation inline, matching the +22 cognitive complexity delta; extracting a small query-param parsing helper would keep the route thin.
Adds flask-limiter imports (+2 imports) but the truncated diff shows no requirements.txt update; confirm the new dependency is declared or deployment will break.
JWT is decoded twice per authenticated request (token_required + _rate_limit_key), and each /tasks page adds a COUNT(*) query; negligible at this scale but worth noting.

Rate-limit storage defaults to redis://localhost:6379/0 — if Redis is unavailable the app errors on requests; an in-memory fallback or startup guard would harden it (fine given the story's hardcoded-6379 infra).

strengths: Keyset (cursor) pagination with ORDER BY id DESC + id < cursor avoids offset pitfalls, and the limit+1 fetch for has_more is correct; next_cursor is derived from the last returned row.
Per-user rate limiting keys on the decoded JWT sub with an IP fallback for auth endpoints, a proper 429 error handler, and env-configurable storage.
Test isolation is handled well: memory:// storage set before import and limiter.reset() in the fixture, keeping rate limits out of real Redis.
Repository additions (list_for_owner_page, count_for_owner) reuse the existing _connection() and param-binding pattern, respecting current conventions.
Comprehensive pagination tests cover default limit, custom limit, clamping, full page-walk, and null terminal cursor.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested, architecturally sound addition of per-user rate limiting and correct keyset pagination that respects existing repository patterns; the mechanical convention score of 0.71 understates the commit because the flagged violations are pre-existing in files not touched by this diff (celery_config.py, tasks.py) or checker artifacts (no new classes defined), while the new code itself adheres to snake_case/UPPER_CASE naming.

compounding_issues: Session 1 greenfield discarded the seed's JWT/auth scaffolding wholesale (the bad-seed seed used static-salt sha256 hashing, so the rebuild was partly justified), forcing Session 2 to re-implement JWT + User model from scratch instead of building on it — visible rework cost (cost + tokens nearly doubled from S1).

Session 3 introduced a hard Celery/Redis broker dependency (redis://localhost:6379/0); the async email path is only exercised via mocking in tests and never runs against a live worker, so the integration is unverified end-to-end.

Session 5's Flask-Limiter default storage_uri points at Redis while tests require RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE_URI=memory:// to be set before app import — an order-sensitive test fixture that is easy to break and reflects the 12 retries / 64 tool-call struggle in that session.
key_decisions: Session 1 rebuilt the codebase flat (single app.py, ~118 LOC, no Blueprints) instead of adopting the modular Blueprint structure from the seed, establishing a simple CRUD core that later sessions layered onto.
Session 2 selected JWT (HS256, werkzeug bcrypt hashing) over the seed's token-table approach, adding a bearer-token auth decorator reused by every subsequent session.
Session 3 chose Celery + Redis for async notifications with env-var-driven REDIS_URL, keeping the request path non-blocking and leaving the app testable via monkeypatched task calls.

Session 4 extracted the Repository pattern (BaseRepository ABC + Task/User repos) so routes never touch raw SQL; it also added owner-scoped and pageable queries that Session 5's cursor pagination directly reused.
Session 5 implemented keyset (cursor-based) pagination with next_cursor and a per-user rate-limit key derived from the JWT sub claim, retrofitting production hardening onto the S4 layering.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions. Tests never regressed (10/10 → 21/21 → 26/26 → 26/26 → 37/37 passing) while code and test volume grew steadily (118 → 444 code lines, 101 → 456 test lines, ending at a near-1:1 test/code ratio of 0.999). Session 1 delivered a minimal but green core; Session 2 added authentication cleanly; Session 3 wired in async notifications; Session 4 was the architectural peak, shrinking app.py by ~90 lines by extracting a proper repository layer that both improved separation of concerns and prepared the data-access methods Session 5 consumed. Session 5 was the sharpest effort spike — 12 retries, 64 tool calls, 305s, and ~5x the per-session cost of S1–S4 (vs 0–1 retries before) — reflecting the difficulty of integrating Flask-Limiter with Redis-backed storage, but it resolved with all 37 tests green and the pagination/rate-limiting correctly per-user. The only flat spot is Session 4, which held the test count at 26 (pure refactor), and the only weakness is that external infra (Celery/Redis) is test-only, never exercised against a live worker.
story_review.summary: A textbook-high-coherence story arc (greenfield → auth → async integration → repository refactor → cross-cutting hardening) in which the agent consistently improved code quality and test coverage every session, with the sole material cost being Session 1's seed discard that forced JWT rework and Session 5's disproportionate struggle with Redis-backed rate limiting.
